HARDWARE EXPLAINED

Read the spec sheet. Then read between the numbers.

Payload, runtime, degrees of freedom: what the headline figures leave unanswered.

H
HUMANOID EditorialResearch, hardware & practical perspectives
EDITORIAL DATE5 Oct 20264 min read

Payload figures need posture and measurement conditions to become useful. · Original illustration by HUMANOID Editorial.

IN THIS STORY
01Ask what the payload means02Give runtime a workload03Treat degrees of freedom as a design description04Keep an evidence column05Translate every important number into a question06Compare configurations before comparing columns07Distinguish dimensions from usable workspace08Keep a small specification audit trail→Your next stepExplore hardware ↗
THE KEY IDEA

A specification becomes useful when you know its configuration, test conditions, and relevance to your task.

Specifications compress a complex machine into a few numbers. That is useful for discovery, but it can hide the conditions behind the measurement. The goal is not to collect the highest values. It is to understand which figures describe the operating conditions you actually expect.

01

Ask what the payload means

Check whether the stated payload is per arm or total, whether it is sustained or momentary, and where the object is held. Reach and posture can change what a useful handling task looks like. Ask the manufacturer to demonstrate the exact combination of object, motion, and duration you require.

02

Give runtime a workload

Standing, walking, manipulating, and running onboard computation are different operating conditions. A runtime figure without a workload is difficult to use in planning. Request the test scenario, charging approach, and any battery exchange procedure. Then map those conditions onto a typical working cycle.

03

Treat degrees of freedom as a design description

A joint count describes aspects of a mechanism, not its ability to complete your application. It does not replace information about joint limits, control access, sensing, or hand design. A platform with fewer joints can still suit a specific task better if its reach and interfaces match the job.

04

Keep an evidence column

Add a source URL, configuration, and review date beside each value in your comparison sheet. Distinguish manufacturer-stated figures from your own measurements. Where conditions are absent, write a question. That habit prevents a tidy spreadsheet from becoming more certain than the underlying information.

05

Translate every important number into a question

Take a proposed shelf-transfer task and annotate its comparison sheet in ordinary language. A reach value becomes a question about reaching the back of the intended shelf from an allowed standing position. A mass value becomes a question about delivery, installation, and the workspace arrangement. A runtime figure becomes a question about completing the planned session with the actual sequence of movement and waiting. This translation does not replace engineering analysis. It makes the purpose of that analysis clear. If nobody can explain how a specification affects the project, keep it as background information rather than allowing it to dominate the purchasing discussion.

06

Compare configurations before comparing columns

A product family can appear across a brochure, a store page, a research paper, and an older demonstration. Create one record for the exact configuration being considered, then attach each source to that record. Note when a detail applies to a different hand, battery arrangement, control edition, or hardware revision. Ask the supplier which document governs the quoted configuration when sources disagree. Leave both observations visible until the discrepancy is resolved. Copying the most attractive number from each page can create an imaginary robot that no one offers. A coherent configuration is more valuable than a spreadsheet containing only the strongest isolated figures.

07

Distinguish dimensions from usable workspace

A diagram can help a team explore whether a platform fits a task, but it is a starting point for a more complete layout. Include the object, fixture, cable routing, approach direction, and places where people need access. For a tabletop example, mark the positions where the object is picked up and released, then consider how the robot moves between them. Ask which motions are represented by the supplier's documentation and which need application-specific evaluation. Keep a sketch alongside the specification sheet. It is often easier to resolve a misunderstanding about operating space when everyone can point to the same proposed arrangement.

08

Keep a small specification audit trail

When an important figure changes, preserve the previous value, its source, and the reason for the update. An engineering team should be able to tell whether it corrected a copying mistake, received a new configuration proposal, or measured something during a trial. Record units explicitly and keep converted values separate from original source values. Add the person who reviewed the entry and the date of that review. This modest discipline becomes especially useful when a project pauses and resumes months later. The next reader can reconstruct what the team actually knew without relying on someone remembering which brochure or conversation supplied a number.

MAKE IT PRACTICAL

Your next step.

  • Record measurement conditions.
  • Check model and hardware revision.
  • Translate each specification into a task requirement.
